newsitem.title: UK: British Conservatives appeal to workers.
newsitem.headline: British Conservatives appeal to workers.

text.p: Britain's ruling Conservatives took their fight for the election to the enemy camp on Friday, appealing to working class trade unionists to join them.
The ruling party, facing an election in the next eight months, is stepping up its attacks on what it sees as the weak points of the opposition Labour party.
Labour, which has a 20 point plus lead in opinion polls, wants to use its annual party conference next week as the launch pad for its election campaign.
But its relations with union leaders have been soured by newspaper reports earlier this month that the opposition party was considering severing its links with the unions.
The reports, based on an off-the-record briefing during the trade unions' annual congress by Labour's employment spokesman Stephen Byers, were immediately denied.
But the row dominated headlines during the unions' annual showcase, souring relations with the party's traditional paymasters and power brokers.

In a rare full-page advert on Friday in the left-leaning Guardian newspaper, whose front page regularly carries Labour adverts inviting people to become members, the Conservatives said: "If Labour don't want you, we do."

Trumpeting union reforms such as mandatory ballots before strike action introduced by the ruling party, the advert said: "The Conservatives introduced democracy into the unions and the madcap schemes of the union bosses were prevented...
"Today new Labour has decided to dump ordinary working men and women as though they were a pair of dirty overalls...
"Working men and women are welcome in the Conservative party...We will not abandon you."

Labour, pointing to former prime minister Margaret Thatcher's attempts to break the power of the unions through such reforms, has always portrayed the ruling party as the foe of ordinary working people and the friend of the rich.
But Thatcher's election victories were achieved at least in part with votes from blue-collar workers who admired her tough, no-compromise style and her championing of personal enterprise.

Apart from the row over union links, the Conservatives are also trying to exploit a feeling expressed by traditional Labour supporters that the opposition has abandoned the party's working class roots and is now looking after the middle class.
Labour leader Tony Blair has dragged the party into the political centre ground since taking over two years ago.
But even with the new advert, the Conservatives face an uphill battle to win over voters.

They face further turmoil at their own annual conference a week after Labour, when the chronic party divisions over Europe are expected to surface again despite desperate attempts by Prime Minister John Major to impose discipline.

Ministers are being expected to submit all speeches at the conference, including those on the fringes, for central approval after a damaging squabble between so-called Eurosceptics opposed to European integration and pro-Europeans in the party.
